# SCA rule reference

<!-- Generated by `npm run catalog` from src/core/rules/registry.ts. Do not edit by hand. -->

Every rule SCA reports, with a description in our own words. In VS Code, hover a finding or run
**SCA: Explain Rule** to see the same text.

## Run-time errors

| Rule | What it finds | Default |
|---|---|---|
| [`runtime-bugfinder:div-zero`](#runtime-bugfinderdiv-zero) | A division or remainder whose divisor can be 0. | on |
| [`runtime-bugfinder:null-deref`](#runtime-bugfindernull-deref) | A pointer that can be NULL is dereferenced (*p, p->f, p[i]). | on |
| [`runtime-bugfinder:uninit-read`](#runtime-bugfinderuninit-read) | A local variable is read before it is set on some path. | on |
| [`runtime-bugfinder:out-of-bounds`](#runtime-bugfinderout-of-bounds) | An array is indexed outside its size, or memcpy / memset / memmove writes past its end. | on |
| [`runtime-bugfinder:overflow`](#runtime-bugfinderoverflow) | Signed arithmetic gives a result outside its type, or a cast to a narrower signed type does not fit. | on |
| [`runtime-bugfinder:uint-wrap`](#runtime-bugfinderuint-wrap) | An unsigned counter is stepped past 0 or past its maximum and wraps around. | on |
| [`runtime-bugfinder:invalid-shift`](#runtime-bugfinderinvalid-shift) | A shift by a negative amount, or by the bit width of the type or more. | on |
| [`runtime-bugfinder:conversion`](#runtime-bugfinderconversion) | A value that can be negative is cast to an unsigned type. | on |
| [`runtime-bugfinder:dead-code`](#runtime-bugfinderdead-code) | A branch that is never taken, or code that can never be reached. | on |
| [`runtime-bugfinder:endless-loop`](#runtime-bugfinderendless-loop) | A loop whose condition is always true, or a wait loop with no way out. | on |
| [`runtime-bugfinder:stack-escape`](#runtime-bugfinderstack-escape) | A function returns the address of one of its local variables. | on |

### runtime-bugfinder:div-zero

**Division by zero.** A division or remainder whose divisor can be 0.

*Why:* Dividing an integer by 0 is undefined behavior: most targets trap, some return garbage.

*Fix:* Check the divisor before dividing, or make sure every caller passes a non-zero value.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
int ratio(int a, int b)
{
    return a / b;
}

/* follows the rule */
int ratio(int a, int b)
{
    if (b == 0) {
        return 0;
    }
    return a / b;
}
```

### runtime-bugfinder:null-deref

**Null pointer dereference.** A pointer that can be NULL is dereferenced (*p, p->f, p[i]).

*Why:* Reading or writing through NULL is undefined behavior; on a microcontroller it may silently touch address 0.

*Fix:* Test the pointer before use, or guarantee it can never be NULL at this point.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
int first(void)
{
    int *p = 0;
    return *p;
}

/* follows the rule */
int first(const int *p)
{
    if (p == 0) {
        return 0;
    }
    return *p;
}
```

### runtime-bugfinder:uninit-read

**Read of an uninitialized variable.** A local variable is read before it is set on some path.

*Why:* An uninitialized local holds whatever was on the stack, so the result changes from run to run.

*Fix:* Initialize the variable at its declaration, or set it on every path before it is read.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
int pick(int c)
{
    int x;
    if (c > 0) {
        x = 1;
    }
    return x;
}

/* follows the rule */
int pick(int c)
{
    int x = 0;
    if (c > 0) {
        x = 1;
    }
    return x;
}
```

### runtime-bugfinder:out-of-bounds

**Array index out of bounds.** An array is indexed outside its size, or memcpy / memset / memmove writes past its end.

*Why:* Accessing past the end of an array corrupts neighboring data or reads garbage; it is undefined behavior.

*Fix:* Check the index against the array size before the access.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
int last(void)
{
    int a[4] = {0};
    return a[4];
}

/* follows the rule */
int last(void)
{
    int a[4] = {0};
    return a[3];
}
```

### runtime-bugfinder:overflow

**Signed integer overflow.** Signed arithmetic gives a result outside its type, or a cast to a narrower signed type does not fit.

*Why:* Signed overflow is undefined behavior; compilers may optimize on the assumption that it never happens.

*Fix:* Check the operands before the operation, or compute in a wider type and range-check the result.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
int next(void)
{
    int x = 2147483647;
    return x + 1;
}

/* follows the rule */
int next(void)
{
    int x = 2147483646;
    return x + 1;
}
```

### runtime-bugfinder:uint-wrap

**Unsigned wrap-around.** An unsigned counter is stepped past 0 or past its maximum and wraps around.

*Why:* Unsigned arithmetic wraps silently; a counter that goes below 0 becomes a huge number.

*Fix:* Test the value before stepping it.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
unsigned int down(void)
{
    unsigned int x = 0U;
    x--;
    return x;
}

/* follows the rule */
unsigned int down(unsigned int x)
{
    if (x > 0U) {
        x--;
    }
    return x;
}
```

### runtime-bugfinder:invalid-shift

**Invalid shift amount.** A shift by a negative amount, or by the bit width of the type or more.

*Why:* Such shifts are undefined behavior; different CPUs give different results.

*Fix:* Keep the shift amount between 0 and the bit width minus one.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
unsigned int top(unsigned int x)
{
    return x << 32;
}

/* follows the rule */
unsigned int top(unsigned int x)
{
    return x << 31;
}
```

### runtime-bugfinder:conversion

**Negative value converted to unsigned.** A value that can be negative is cast to an unsigned type.

*Why:* The cast turns -1 into the largest unsigned value, which then passes range checks it should fail.

*Fix:* Check that the value is not negative before the cast.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
unsigned int as_count(int x)
{
    return (unsigned int)x;
}

/* follows the rule */
unsigned int as_count(int x)
{
    if (x < 0) {
        return 0U;
    }
    return (unsigned int)x;
}
```

### runtime-bugfinder:dead-code

**Dead code.** A branch that is never taken, or code that can never be reached.

*Why:* Dead code is untested by definition and often shows that a condition is not what the author meant.

*Fix:* Fix the condition, or remove the code that cannot run.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
int sign(void)
{
    int x = 0;
    if (x > 0) {
        return 1;
    }
    return 0;
}

/* follows the rule */
int sign(int x)
{
    if (x > 0) {
        return 1;
    }
    return 0;
}
```

### runtime-bugfinder:endless-loop

**Endless loop.** A loop whose condition is always true, or a wait loop with no way out.

*Why:* A loop that never ends hangs the task; in a wait loop a hardware fault becomes a lock-up.

*Fix:* Add a timeout or an exit condition that can become true.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
void count(void)
{
    unsigned char i;
    for (i = 0U; i < 300U; i++) {
    }
}

/* follows the rule */
void count(void)
{
    unsigned int i;
    for (i = 0U; i < 300U; i++) {
    }
}
```

### runtime-bugfinder:stack-escape

**Address of a local returned.** A function returns the address of one of its local variables.

*Why:* The local's memory is reused after the function returns, so the pointer points to garbage.

*Fix:* Return the value, use a static or caller-provided buffer instead.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
int *make(void)
{
    int x = 1;
    return &x;
}

/* follows the rule */
int *make(void)
{
    static int x = 1;
    return &x;
}
```

## Memory lifetime

| Rule | What it finds | Default |
|---|---|---|
| [`runtime-bugfinder:memory-leak`](#runtime-bugfindermemory-leak) | The function returns (or ends) while it still owns memory it allocated, and no pointer to it is kept. | on |
| [`runtime-bugfinder:double-free`](#runtime-bugfinderdouble-free) | free() is called on memory that was already freed. | on |
| [`runtime-bugfinder:use-after-free`](#runtime-bugfinderuse-after-free) | Memory is read or written through a pointer after it was freed. | on |
| [`runtime-bugfinder:bad-free`](#runtime-bugfinderbad-free) | free() is called on an array, the address of a variable or a string literal. | on |
| [`runtime-bugfinder:dangling-pointer`](#runtime-bugfinderdangling-pointer) | A pointer to a local array is used after the block that declares the array has ended. | on |
| [`runtime-bugfinder:unchecked-alloc`](#runtime-bugfinderunchecked-alloc) | The result of malloc(), calloc() or realloc() is used without testing it against NULL. | on |
| [`runtime-bugfinder:alloc-size`](#runtime-bugfinderalloc-size) | malloc(n) is stored as a pointer to values wider than a byte, but n is not multiplied by the element size. | on |
| [`runtime-bugfinder:sizeof-pointer`](#runtime-bugfindersizeof-pointer) | sizeof(p) of a pointer p is used as the size of the memory p points to (memset, memcpy, malloc, ...). | on |
| [`runtime-bugfinder:pointer-arith`](#runtime-bugfinderpointer-arith) | Adding to (or subtracting from) a pointer into an array gives a pointer before its start or more than one past its end. | on |

### runtime-bugfinder:memory-leak

**Memory leak.** The function returns (or ends) while it still owns memory it allocated, and no pointer to it is kept.

*Why:* The memory can never be freed again. In a long-running program each leak shrinks the heap until an allocation fails.

*Fix:* Free the memory on every path that does not hand it on, or store it where it is freed later.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
int sum(int n)
{
    int *buf = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    if (buf == 0) {
        return 0;
    }
    buf[0] = n;
    return buf[0];
}

/* follows the rule */
int sum(int n)
{
    int *buf = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    int r;
    if (buf == 0) {
        return 0;
    }
    buf[0] = n;
    r = buf[0];
    free(buf);
    return r;
}
```

### runtime-bugfinder:double-free

**Double free.** free() is called on memory that was already freed.

*Why:* Freeing twice corrupts the heap's bookkeeping; later allocations can return memory that is still in use.

*Fix:* Set the pointer to NULL right after free() (free(NULL) does nothing), or make sure only one owner frees it.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
void twice(void)
{
    char *p = malloc(16);
    free(p);
    free(p);
}

/* follows the rule */
void twice(void)
{
    char *p = malloc(16);
    free(p);
    p = 0;
    free(p);
}
```

### runtime-bugfinder:use-after-free

**Use after free.** Memory is read or written through a pointer after it was freed.

*Why:* Freed memory belongs to the allocator again: it may already hold other data, so the read gives garbage and the write corrupts it.

*Fix:* Copy what you still need before free(), and free the memory last.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
int last(void)
{
    int *p = malloc(sizeof(int));
    if (p == 0) {
        return 0;
    }
    *p = 1;
    free(p);
    return *p;
}

/* follows the rule */
int last(void)
{
    int *p = malloc(sizeof(int));
    int v;
    if (p == 0) {
        return 0;
    }
    *p = 1;
    v = *p;
    free(p);
    return v;
}
```

### runtime-bugfinder:bad-free

**Free of memory not from malloc.** free() is called on an array, the address of a variable or a string literal.

*Why:* free() only accepts pointers that malloc(), calloc() or realloc() returned; anything else corrupts the heap.

*Fix:* Only free what was allocated; static and local objects need no free().

```c
/* breaks the rule */
static char pool[32];

void release(void)
{
    free(pool);
}

/* follows the rule */
static char *pool;

void release(void)
{
    free(pool);
    pool = 0;
}
```

### runtime-bugfinder:dangling-pointer

**Dangling pointer to a local array.** A pointer to a local array is used after the block that declares the array has ended.

*Why:* The array's memory is reused once its block ends, so the pointer reads whatever is there now.

*Fix:* Declare the array in the outer block, or make it static.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
int pick(int mode)
{
    const int *t = 0;
    if (mode != 0) {
        int local[2] = {1, 2};
        t = local;
    }
    return (t != 0) ? t[1] : 0;
}

/* follows the rule */
int pick(int mode)
{
    const int *t = 0;
    if (mode != 0) {
        static const int local[2] = {1, 2};
        t = local;
    }
    return (t != 0) ? t[1] : 0;
}
```

### runtime-bugfinder:unchecked-alloc

**Allocation result not checked.** The result of malloc(), calloc() or realloc() is used without testing it against NULL.

*Why:* Allocations fail when memory runs out; the NULL result is then dereferenced.

*Fix:* Test the pointer before the first use and handle the failure.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
int *make(void)
{
    int *p = malloc(sizeof(int));
    *p = 0;
    return p;
}

/* follows the rule */
int *make(void)
{
    int *p = malloc(sizeof(int));
    if (p != 0) {
        *p = 0;
    }
    return p;
}
```

### runtime-bugfinder:alloc-size

**Allocation size not in elements.** malloc(n) is stored as a pointer to values wider than a byte, but n is not multiplied by the element size.

*Why:* malloc() counts bytes. Allocating n bytes for n 16-bit values gives half the memory, and writing the last values overflows the block.

*Fix:* Multiply the count by sizeof the element: malloc(n * sizeof(*p)).

```c
/* breaks the rule */
unsigned short *table(unsigned int n)
{
    unsigned short *t = (unsigned short *)malloc(n);
    return t;
}

/* follows the rule */
unsigned short *table(unsigned int n)
{
    unsigned short *t = (unsigned short *)malloc(n * sizeof(unsigned short));
    return t;
}
```

### runtime-bugfinder:sizeof-pointer

**sizeof of a pointer used as a buffer size.** sizeof(p) of a pointer p is used as the size of the memory p points to (memset, memcpy, malloc, ...).

*Why:* sizeof(p) is the size of the pointer itself (4 or 8 bytes), not of the table or buffer, so only part of it is cleared or copied.

*Fix:* Use the object's size: sizeof(*p) times the element count, or sizeof of the array itself.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
void clear(int *table)
{
    memset(table, 0, sizeof(table));
}

/* follows the rule */
void clear(int *table, unsigned int n)
{
    memset(table, 0, n * sizeof(*table));
}
```

### runtime-bugfinder:pointer-arith

**Pointer arithmetic out of bounds.** Adding to (or subtracting from) a pointer into an array gives a pointer before its start or more than one past its end.

*Why:* Such a pointer is undefined behavior even before it is dereferenced, and any use of it reads or writes outside the array.

*Fix:* Check the offset against the array length before computing the pointer.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
static char line[16];

const char *after(unsigned int n)
{
    return line + n;
}

/* follows the rule */
static char line[16];

const char *after(unsigned int n)
{
    if (n > 16U) {
        n = 16U;
    }
    return line + n;
}
```

## Functions and values

| Rule | What it finds | Default |
|---|---|---|
| [`runtime-bugfinder:missing-return`](#runtime-bugfindermissing-return) | A function that returns a value can reach the end of its body without a return statement. | on |
| [`runtime-bugfinder:invalid-enum`](#runtime-bugfinderinvalid-enum) | An integer is cast to an enum type, but its value can be outside the range of the enum's constants. | on |
| [`runtime-bugfinder:no-return-call`](#runtime-bugfinderno-return-call) | A function of the file can never return (an endless loop, or every path stops the program), but it is not declared _Noreturn. | on |
| [`runtime-bugfinder:bad-function-pointer`](#runtime-bugfinderbad-function-pointer) | A function pointer is made by casting the address of a data object (an array, a variable) and then called. | on |

### runtime-bugfinder:missing-return

**Missing return value.** A function that returns a value can reach the end of its body without a return statement.

*Why:* The caller then uses whatever happens to be in the return register: undefined behavior that often looks like a random value.

*Fix:* Return a value on every path, for example a safe default after a switch.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
int sign(int x)
{
    if (x > 0) {
        return 1;
    } else if (x < 0) {
        return -1;
    }
}

/* follows the rule */
int sign(int x)
{
    if (x > 0) {
        return 1;
    } else if (x < 0) {
        return -1;
    }
    return 0;
}
```

### runtime-bugfinder:invalid-enum

**Invalid enum value.** An integer is cast to an enum type, but its value can be outside the range of the enum's constants.

*Why:* Code that switches on the enum assumes one of its constants; an out-of-range value takes a path nobody planned for.

*Fix:* Check the integer against the enum's range before the cast, and map bad values to a safe constant.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
typedef enum { RED = 0, GREEN = 1, BLUE = 2 } Color;

Color color_of(unsigned char raw)
{
    return (Color)raw;
}

/* follows the rule */
typedef enum { RED = 0, GREEN = 1, BLUE = 2 } Color;

Color color_of(unsigned char raw)
{
    if (raw > 2U) {
        return RED;
    }
    return (Color)raw;
}
```

### runtime-bugfinder:no-return-call

**Call to a function that never returns.** A function of the file can never return (an endless loop, or every path stops the program), but it is not declared _Noreturn.

*Why:* Readers and tools expect the code after the call to run. A hidden endless loop also hangs the program in a way that is easy to miss (for example until a watchdog reset).

*Fix:* Declare the function _Noreturn (or with a noreturn attribute) when that is intended; otherwise give it a way out.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
static void halt(void)
{
    for (;;) {
    }
}

void check(int ok)
{
    if (ok == 0) {
        halt();
    }
}

/* follows the rule */
static void halt(void)
{
    for (;;) {
        if (stop_requested() != 0) {
            return;
        }
    }
}

void check(int ok)
{
    if (ok == 0) {
        halt();
    }
}
```

### runtime-bugfinder:bad-function-pointer

**Call through a function pointer made from data.** A function pointer is made by casting the address of a data object (an array, a variable) and then called.

*Why:* Data memory does not hold code for this function; the call jumps into the data, which crashes or runs garbage (and is often blocked by the memory protection).

*Fix:* Point the function pointer to a real function. Calling code at a fixed address (a boot loader) should use that address as a constant, with a justification.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
typedef int (*Handler)(int);
static unsigned char code_buf[64];

int run(int x)
{
    Handler h = (Handler)(void *)code_buf;
    return h(x);
}

/* follows the rule */
typedef int (*Handler)(int);

static int twice(int x)
{
    return 2 * x;
}

int run(int x)
{
    Handler h = twice;
    return h(x);
}
```

## Strings and formats

| Rule | What it finds | Default |
|---|---|---|
| [`runtime-bugfinder:string-overflow`](#runtime-bugfinderstring-overflow) | strcpy(), strcat(), sprintf() or strncpy() can write more characters than the destination array holds. | on |
| [`runtime-bugfinder:missing-terminator`](#runtime-bugfindermissing-terminator) | strncpy() may fill the whole destination array, so a long source leaves it without the terminating 0. | on |
| [`runtime-bugfinder:overlapping-copy`](#runtime-bugfinderoverlapping-copy) | memcpy(), strcpy() or sprintf() reads from memory it is writing to. | on |
| [`runtime-bugfinder:format-mismatch`](#runtime-bugfinderformat-mismatch) | A conversion in a printf-style format does not fit the type of its argument (%d with a float, %f with an int, %s with a number), or the argument is missing. | on |
| [`runtime-bugfinder:uncontrolled-format`](#runtime-bugfinderuncontrolled-format) | The format of a printf-style call is a variable (a parameter, a buffer) and no other arguments are passed. | on |

### runtime-bugfinder:string-overflow

**String buffer overflow.** strcpy(), strcat(), sprintf() or strncpy() can write more characters than the destination array holds.

*Why:* These functions do not know the size of the destination; a long input writes past its end and corrupts the memory next to it.

*Fix:* Use a bounded call (snprintf() with the buffer size, or strncpy() with size - 1 and a terminating 0) and check the input length.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
static char name[8];

void set_name(const char *s)
{
    (void)strcpy(name, s);
}

/* follows the rule */
static char name[8];

void set_name(const char *s)
{
    (void)strncpy(name, s, sizeof(name) - 1U);
    name[sizeof(name) - 1U] = '\0';
}
```

### runtime-bugfinder:missing-terminator

**String without terminating 0.** strncpy() may fill the whole destination array, so a long source leaves it without the terminating 0.

*Why:* Code that reads the array as a string then runs past its end, until some 0 byte happens to follow.

*Fix:* Copy at most size - 1 bytes and set the last byte to 0 right after the copy.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
void copy(char *out, const char *s)
{
    char tmp[12];
    (void)strncpy(tmp, s, sizeof(tmp));
    out[0] = tmp[0];
}

/* follows the rule */
void copy(char *out, const char *s)
{
    char tmp[12];
    (void)strncpy(tmp, s, sizeof(tmp));
    tmp[sizeof(tmp) - 1U] = '\0';
    out[0] = tmp[0];
}
```

### runtime-bugfinder:overlapping-copy

**Overlapping copy.** memcpy(), strcpy() or sprintf() reads from memory it is writing to.

*Why:* These functions are undefined when source and destination overlap; optimized versions copy in blocks and can scramble the data.

*Fix:* Use memmove() for overlapping blocks, or copy through a separate buffer.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
static char rows[4][16];

void shift(void)
{
    (void)memcpy(rows[0], rows[1], 3U * 16U);
}

/* follows the rule */
static char rows[4][16];

void shift(void)
{
    (void)memmove(rows[0], rows[1], 3U * 16U);
}
```

### runtime-bugfinder:format-mismatch

**printf format does not match the argument.** A conversion in a printf-style format does not fit the type of its argument (%d with a float, %f with an int, %s with a number), or the argument is missing.

*Why:* printf() reads the arguments by the format: a wrong type reads the wrong bytes, and a missing argument reads garbage from the stack.

*Fix:* Use the conversion for the argument's type, or cast the argument: (int)x for %d, (double)x for %f.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
void show(float t)
{
    (void)printf("%d\n", t);
}

/* follows the rule */
void show(float t)
{
    (void)printf("%d\n", (int)t);
}
```

### runtime-bugfinder:uncontrolled-format

**Format string from a variable.** The format of a printf-style call is a variable (a parameter, a buffer) and no other arguments are passed.

*Why:* If the text contains '%', printf() reads arguments that do not exist; with %n it even writes to memory. Text from a tester or a bus must never be a format.

*Fix:* Pass the text as an argument: printf("%s", msg).

```c
/* breaks the rule */
void say(const char *msg)
{
    (void)printf(msg);
}

/* follows the rule */
void say(const char *msg)
{
    (void)printf("%s", msg);
}
```

## Floating point

| Rule | What it finds | Default |
|---|---|---|
| [`runtime-bugfinder:float-overflow`](#runtime-bugfinderfloat-overflow) | exp() or expf() gets an argument so large that the result is infinite (above about 88 for float, 709 for double). | on |
| [`runtime-bugfinder:float-invalid`](#runtime-bugfinderfloat-invalid) | sqrt() of a negative value, log() of 0 or a negative value, or acos() / asin() outside [-1, 1]. | on |
| [`runtime-bugfinder:float-conversion`](#runtime-bugfinderfloat-conversion) | A floating-point value is cast to an integer type that cannot hold it. | on |

### runtime-bugfinder:float-overflow

**Floating-point overflow.** exp() or expf() gets an argument so large that the result is infinite (above about 88 for float, 709 for double).

*Why:* An infinite value spreads through the following math (inf - inf is NaN) and usually ends in a wrong output or a failed check much later.

*Fix:* Clamp the argument to a safe range before the call.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
float grow(float t)
{
    return expf(t * 0.5f);
}

/* follows the rule */
float grow(float t)
{
    if (t > 100.0f) {
        t = 100.0f;
    }
    return expf(t * 0.5f);
}
```

### runtime-bugfinder:float-invalid

**Invalid floating-point operation.** sqrt() of a negative value, log() of 0 or a negative value, or acos() / asin() outside [-1, 1].

*Why:* The result is NaN (or -infinity), and every comparison with NaN is false, so later range checks let it through.

*Fix:* Check the argument's range first and handle the invalid case.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
float root(float p)
{
    return sqrtf(p);
}

/* follows the rule */
float root(float p)
{
    if (p < 0.0f) {
        return 0.0f;
    }
    return sqrtf(p);
}
```

### runtime-bugfinder:float-conversion

**Float to integer conversion out of range.** A floating-point value is cast to an integer type that cannot hold it.

*Why:* Converting a float that does not fit the integer type is undefined behavior: targets saturate, wrap or produce a trap value.

*Fix:* Clamp the value to the integer type's range (and handle NaN) before the cast.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
short to_raw(float x)
{
    return (short)(x * 100.0f);
}

/* follows the rule */
short to_raw(float x)
{
    if (x > 300.0f) {
        x = 300.0f;
    } else if (x < -300.0f) {
        x = -300.0f;
    }
    return (short)(x * 100.0f);
}
```

## Expressions

| Rule | What it finds | Default |
|---|---|---|
| [`sca-own:float-equality`](#sca-ownfloat-equality) | Floating-point values are compared with == or !=. | on |
| [`sca-own:assignment-in-condition`](#sca-ownassignment-in-condition) | An assignment inside the condition of if, while, for or ?:. | on |
| [`sca-own:assignment-as-value`](#sca-ownassignment-as-value) | The result of an assignment is used inside a larger expression (a = b = 0, f(x = 3)). | on |
| [`sca-own:side-effect-in-logical`](#sca-ownside-effect-in-logical) | ++, -- or an assignment in the right operand of && or ||. | on |
| [`sca-own:increment-in-expression`](#sca-ownincrement-in-expression) | ++ or -- is part of a larger expression (a[i++] = x). | off |
| [`sca-own:comma-operator`](#sca-owncomma-operator) | The comma operator is used outside a for header. | on |
| [`sca-own:operator-precedence`](#sca-ownoperator-precedence) | Bitwise operators mixed with comparisons, shifts or arithmetic, or && mixed with ||, without parentheses. | on |
| [`sca-own:sizeof-side-effect`](#sca-ownsizeof-side-effect) | sizeof is applied to an expression with ++, --, an assignment or a call. | on |

### sca-own:float-equality

**Floating-point equality.** Floating-point values are compared with == or !=.

*Why:* Rounding makes two computations of the same value differ in the last bits, so exact equality is rarely true when it should be.

*Fix:* Compare the difference with a tolerance: fabsf(a - b) < EPS.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
int same(float a, float b)
{
    return a == b;
}

/* follows the rule */
int same(float a, float b)
{
    float d = a - b;
    return (d < 0.001f) && (d > -0.001f);
}
```

### sca-own:assignment-in-condition

**Assignment in a condition.** An assignment inside the condition of if, while, for or ?:.

*Why:* It is easy to read as a comparison, and = typed instead of == is a classic bug.

*Fix:* Assign first, then test the variable in the condition.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
int ready(int *p, int v)
{
    if ((*p = v) != 0) {
        return 1;
    }
    return 0;
}

/* follows the rule */
int ready(int *p, int v)
{
    *p = v;
    if (*p != 0) {
        return 1;
    }
    return 0;
}
```

### sca-own:assignment-as-value

**Assignment used as a value.** The result of an assignment is used inside a larger expression (a = b = 0, f(x = 3)).

*Why:* Hidden assignments make an expression do two things at once and hide where a variable changes.

*Fix:* Write each assignment as its own statement.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
void reset(int *a, int *b)
{
    *a = *b = 0;
}

/* follows the rule */
void reset(int *a, int *b)
{
    *b = 0;
    *a = 0;
}
```

### sca-own:side-effect-in-logical

**Side effect in the right operand of && or ||.** ++, -- or an assignment in the right operand of && or ||.

*Why:* The right operand only runs when the left one does not decide the result, so the side effect happens only sometimes.

*Fix:* Move the side effect out of the condition.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
int over(unsigned int len, unsigned int *seen)
{
    return (len == 0U) || ((*seen)++ > 10U);
}

/* follows the rule */
int over(unsigned int len, unsigned int *seen)
{
    unsigned int before = *seen;
    *seen = before + 1U;
    return (len == 0U) || (before > 10U);
}
```

### sca-own:increment-in-expression

**Increment or decrement inside an expression.** ++ or -- is part of a larger expression (a[i++] = x).

*Why:* Mixing the change of a variable with its use makes the order of effects hard to see and easy to get wrong.

*Fix:* Do the increment or decrement as its own statement.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
void put(int *a, int *n, int v)
{
    a[(*n)++] = v;
}

/* follows the rule */
void put(int *a, int *n, int v)
{
    a[*n] = v;
    *n = *n + 1;
}
```

### sca-own:comma-operator

**Comma operator.** The comma operator is used outside a for header.

*Why:* It packs several actions into one expression and is often a typo for a semicolon or a parameter list.

*Fix:* Write the expressions as separate statements.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
void both(int *a, int *b)
{
    *a = 1, *b = 2;
}

/* follows the rule */
void both(int *a, int *b)
{
    *a = 1;
    *b = 2;
}
```

### sca-own:operator-precedence

**Unclear operator precedence.** Bitwise operators mixed with comparisons, shifts or arithmetic, or && mixed with ||, without parentheses.

*Why:* C's precedence for these operators surprises people: a & b == c tests b == c first.

*Fix:* Add parentheses that show the intended grouping.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
int locked(unsigned int flags)
{
    return flags & 4U != 0U;
}

/* follows the rule */
int locked(unsigned int flags)
{
    return (flags & 4U) != 0U;
}
```

### sca-own:sizeof-side-effect

**Side effect inside sizeof.** sizeof is applied to an expression with ++, --, an assignment or a call.

*Why:* sizeof does not evaluate its operand, so the side effect never happens.

*Fix:* Do the side effect separately and apply sizeof to a plain expression or a type.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
unsigned long size(int i)
{
    return sizeof(i++);
}

/* follows the rule */
unsigned long size(int i)
{
    return sizeof(i);
}
```

## Control flow

| Rule | What it finds | Default |
|---|---|---|
| [`sca-own:switch-default`](#sca-ownswitch-default) | A switch statement has no default clause. | on |
| [`sca-own:goto`](#sca-owngoto) | A goto statement is used. | on |
| [`sca-own:switch-fallthrough`](#sca-ownswitch-fallthrough) | A case with statements does not end with break, return, continue or goto, so it falls into the next case. | on |
| [`sca-own:missing-braces`](#sca-ownmissing-braces) | The body of if, else, for, while or do is not a { } block. | on |
| [`sca-own:empty-body`](#sca-ownempty-body) | if, else, for or while has a lone ; as its body. | on |
| [`sca-own:else-if-without-else`](#sca-ownelse-if-without-else) | An if ... else if chain ends without an else. | on |
| [`sca-own:loop-float-counter`](#sca-ownloop-float-counter) | A for loop counts with a floating-point variable. | on |
| [`sca-own:loop-counter-modified`](#sca-ownloop-counter-modified) | The counter of a for loop is also changed inside the loop body. | on |
| [`sca-own:switch-too-few-cases`](#sca-ownswitch-too-few-cases) | A switch has no clause or only one. | on |
| [`sca-own:switch-on-boolean`](#sca-ownswitch-on-boolean) | A switch tests a boolean expression (a comparison or a bool variable). | on |
| [`sca-own:invariant-condition`](#sca-owninvariant-condition) | An if condition is always true or always false (e.g. a u8 compared with 255). | on |
| [`sca-own:recursion`](#sca-ownrecursion) | A function calls itself, directly or through other functions of the same file. | on |

### sca-own:switch-default

**switch without default.** A switch statement has no default clause.

*Why:* Values that no case expects then pass silently; a default clause handles them on purpose.

*Fix:* Add a default clause that handles (or reports) unexpected values.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
int power(int m)
{
    int p = 0;
    switch (m) {
    case 1:
        p = 100;
        break;
    case 2:
        p = 10;
        break;
    }
    return p;
}

/* follows the rule */
int power(int m)
{
    int p;
    switch (m) {
    case 1:
        p = 100;
        break;
    case 2:
        p = 10;
        break;
    default:
        p = 0;
        break;
    }
    return p;
}
```

### sca-own:goto

**goto.** A goto statement is used.

*Why:* Jumps make control flow hard to follow, review and analyze.

*Fix:* Restructure with if, loops or an early return.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
int find(const int *v, int n, int x)
{
    int i;
    for (i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (v[i] == x) {
            goto found;
        }
    }
    return -1;
found:
    return i;
}

/* follows the rule */
int find(const int *v, int n, int x)
{
    int i;
    for (i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (v[i] == x) {
            return i;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}
```

### sca-own:switch-fallthrough

**switch fall-through.** A case with statements does not end with break, return, continue or goto, so it falls into the next case.

*Why:* A forgotten break is a common bug; intended fall-through should be visible.

*Fix:* Add the missing break, or mark intended fall-through with a /* fallthrough */ comment.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
int step(int m)
{
    int r = 0;
    switch (m) {
    case 1:
        r = 1;
    case 2:
        r = r + 2;
        break;
    default:
        break;
    }
    return r;
}

/* follows the rule */
int step(int m)
{
    int r = 0;
    switch (m) {
    case 1:
        r = 1;
        break;
    case 2:
        r = r + 2;
        break;
    default:
        break;
    }
    return r;
}
```

### sca-own:missing-braces

**Body without braces.** The body of if, else, for, while or do is not a { } block.

*Why:* A line added later looks like part of the body but is not.

*Fix:* Put the body in braces.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
int clamp(int x)
{
    if (x > 10)
        x = 10;
    return x;
}

/* follows the rule */
int clamp(int x)
{
    if (x > 10) {
        x = 10;
    }
    return x;
}
```

### sca-own:empty-body

**Empty body (stray semicolon).** if, else, for or while has a lone ; as its body.

*Why:* Usually a stray semicolon: the code below then runs every time.

*Fix:* Remove the semicolon; if an empty body is intended, write { } with a comment.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
int clamp(int x)
{
    if (x > 10);
    {
        x = 10;
    }
    return x;
}

/* follows the rule */
int clamp(int x)
{
    if (x > 10) {
        x = 10;
    }
    return x;
}
```

### sca-own:else-if-without-else

**else if chain without final else.** An if ... else if chain ends without an else.

*Why:* Like a switch without default: the remaining cases are not handled on purpose.

*Fix:* Add a final else that handles the rest, or says in a comment why nothing is needed.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
int level(int x)
{
    int r = 0;
    if (x > 10) {
        r = 2;
    } else if (x > 5) {
        r = 1;
    }
    return r;
}

/* follows the rule */
int level(int x)
{
    int r;
    if (x > 10) {
        r = 2;
    } else if (x > 5) {
        r = 1;
    } else {
        r = 0;
    }
    return r;
}
```

### sca-own:loop-float-counter

**Floating-point loop counter.** A for loop counts with a floating-point variable.

*Why:* Rounding makes the number of iterations hard to predict.

*Fix:* Count with an integer and compute the floating-point value from it.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
float sum(void)
{
    float s = 0.0f;
    float x;
    for (x = 0.0f; x < 1.0f; x += 0.1f) {
        s += x;
    }
    return s;
}

/* follows the rule */
float sum(void)
{
    float s = 0.0f;
    int i;
    for (i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
        s += (float)i * 0.1f;
    }
    return s;
}
```

### sca-own:loop-counter-modified

**Loop counter changed in the body.** The counter of a for loop is also changed inside the loop body.

*Why:* Readers expect the for header to say how the loop steps; a second change hides that.

*Fix:* Change the counter only in the header, or use a while loop.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
int skip(const int *v, int n)
{
    int i;
    int s = 0;
    for (i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (v[i] == 0) {
            i++;
        }
        s += v[i];
    }
    return s;
}

/* follows the rule */
int skip(const int *v, int n)
{
    int i;
    int s = 0;
    for (i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (v[i] != 0) {
            s += v[i];
        }
    }
    return s;
}
```

### sca-own:switch-too-few-cases

**switch with fewer than two clauses.** A switch has no clause or only one.

*Why:* An if statement says the same more clearly.

*Fix:* Replace the switch with an if.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
int one(int m)
{
    switch (m) {
    default:
        return 0;
    }
}

/* follows the rule */
int one(int m)
{
    (void)m;
    return 0;
}
```

### sca-own:switch-on-boolean

**switch on a boolean.** A switch tests a boolean expression (a comparison or a bool variable).

*Why:* A boolean has two values; if / else is the natural way to write that.

*Fix:* Use if / else.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
int pos(int x)
{
    switch (x > 0) {
    case 1:
        return 1;
    default:
        return 0;
    }
}

/* follows the rule */
int pos(int x)
{
    if (x > 0) {
        return 1;
    }
    return 0;
}
```

### sca-own:invariant-condition

**Condition that never changes.** An if condition is always true or always false (e.g. a u8 compared with 255).

*Why:* The test is useless, and usually means the author expected another type or value.

*Fix:* Fix the condition or remove it.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
int ok(unsigned char x)
{
    int r;
    if (x <= 255U) {
        r = 1;
    } else {
        r = 0;
    }
    return r;
}

/* follows the rule */
int ok(unsigned char x)
{
    int r;
    if (x <= 200U) {
        r = 1;
    } else {
        r = 0;
    }
    return r;
}
```

### sca-own:recursion

**Recursion.** A function calls itself, directly or through other functions of the same file.

*Why:* Stack use then depends on the input and cannot be bounded when the code is built.

*Fix:* Rewrite the algorithm as a loop.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
unsigned int gcd(unsigned int a, unsigned int b)
{
    if (b == 0U) {
        return a;
    }
    return gcd(b, a % b);
}

/* follows the rule */
unsigned int gcd(unsigned int a, unsigned int b)
{
    while (b != 0U) {
        unsigned int t = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = t;
    }
    return a;
}
```

## Types and literals

| Rule | What it finds | Default |
|---|---|---|
| [`sca-own:octal-constant`](#sca-ownoctal-constant) | An integer constant is written in octal (a leading 0, as in 010). | on |
| [`sca-own:lowercase-suffix`](#sca-ownlowercase-suffix) | A literal suffix uses a lowercase l (10l). | on |
| [`sca-own:unsigned-suffix`](#sca-ownunsigned-suffix) | A hex or octal constant above the signed int range has no U suffix. | on |
| [`sca-own:implicit-conversion`](#sca-ownimplicit-conversion) | An assignment, initialization or return converts a value to a narrower type, or between signed and unsigned, without a cast. | on |
| [`sca-own:signed-unsigned-compare`](#sca-ownsigned-unsigned-compare) | A comparison where a signed value is converted to unsigned. | on |
| [`sca-own:signed-bitwise`](#sca-ownsigned-bitwise) | &, |, ^, ~, << or >> is applied to a signed value. | on |
| [`sca-own:vla`](#sca-ownvla) | An array whose size is only known at run time. | on |
| [`sca-own:bitfield-type`](#sca-ownbitfield-type) | A bit-field is declared with plain int, char, short or long. | on |
| [`sca-own:int-division-to-float`](#sca-ownint-division-to-float) | The result of an integer division is stored as a floating-point value. | on |

### sca-own:octal-constant

**Octal constant.** An integer constant is written in octal (a leading 0, as in 010).

*Why:* 010 is eight, not ten; a leading zero is easy to add by accident.

*Fix:* Write the number in decimal or hex.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
int trim(void)
{
    return 010;
}

/* follows the rule */
int trim(void)
{
    return 10;
}
```

### sca-own:lowercase-suffix

**Lowercase l suffix.** A literal suffix uses a lowercase l (10l).

*Why:* A lowercase l looks like the digit 1.

*Fix:* Write the suffix as L (10L, 10UL).

```c
/* breaks the rule */
long big(void)
{
    return 10l;
}

/* follows the rule */
long big(void)
{
    return 10L;
}
```

### sca-own:unsigned-suffix

**Unsigned constant without U.** A hex or octal constant above the signed int range has no U suffix.

*Why:* Such a constant silently gets an unsigned type, which changes how comparisons and arithmetic behave.

*Fix:* Add a U suffix so the type is visible.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
unsigned int mask(void)
{
    return 0x80000000;
}

/* follows the rule */
unsigned int mask(void)
{
    return 0x80000000U;
}
```

### sca-own:implicit-conversion

**Implicit narrowing or sign change.** An assignment, initialization or return converts a value to a narrower type, or between signed and unsigned, without a cast.

*Why:* High bits are cut off or the sign changes without anything in the code showing it.

*Fix:* Check the range, then convert with an explicit cast.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
short trim(int value)
{
    short t = value;
    return t;
}

/* follows the rule */
short trim(int value)
{
    short t = 0;
    if ((value >= -100) && (value <= 100)) {
        t = (short)value;
    }
    return t;
}
```

### sca-own:signed-unsigned-compare

**Signed / unsigned comparison.** A comparison where a signed value is converted to unsigned.

*Why:* The conversion turns a negative value into a huge one, so -1 < 1U is false.

*Fix:* Check that the signed value is not negative, then cast it.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
int fits(int parsed, unsigned int max_len)
{
    return parsed <= max_len;
}

/* follows the rule */
int fits(int parsed, unsigned int max_len)
{
    return (parsed >= 0) && ((unsigned int)parsed <= max_len);
}
```

### sca-own:signed-bitwise

**Bitwise operation on a signed value.** &, |, ^, ~, << or >> is applied to a signed value.

*Why:* Shifting negative values is undefined or compiler-specific, and bit patterns of signed values depend on their representation.

*Fix:* Do bit operations on unsigned types.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
short half(short trim)
{
    return (short)(trim >> 1);
}

/* follows the rule */
short half(short trim)
{
    return (short)(trim / 2);
}
```

### sca-own:vla

**Variable-length array.** An array whose size is only known at run time.

*Why:* Stack use then depends on the input and cannot be bounded; a large size overflows the stack without warning.

*Fix:* Use a fixed maximum size and check the length against it.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
void copy(const char *s, unsigned int len)
{
    char buf[len + 1U];
    buf[0] = s[0];
}

/* follows the rule */
void copy(const char *s, unsigned int len)
{
    char buf[32];
    if (len < 32U) {
        buf[0] = s[0];
    }
}
```

### sca-own:bitfield-type

**Bit-field with plain int.** A bit-field is declared with plain int, char, short or long.

*Why:* Whether such a bit-field is signed depends on the compiler.

*Fix:* Declare it with an explicitly unsigned (or signed) type.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
struct flags {
    int ready : 1;
};

/* follows the rule */
struct flags {
    unsigned int ready : 1;
};
```

### sca-own:int-division-to-float

**Integer division stored as float.** The result of an integer division is stored as a floating-point value.

*Why:* The division is done in integers first, so the fraction is lost before the conversion.

*Fix:* Cast an operand to float so the division is done in floating point.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
float avg(int sum, int n)
{
    float a = sum / n;
    return a;
}

/* follows the rule */
float avg(int sum, int n)
{
    float a = (float)sum / (float)n;
    return a;
}
```

## Declarations

| Rule | What it finds | Default |
|---|---|---|
| [`sca-own:unused-variable`](#sca-ownunused-variable) | A local variable is declared but never used. | on |
| [`sca-own:unused-parameter`](#sca-ownunused-parameter) | A function parameter is never used. | on |
| [`sca-own:shadowing`](#sca-ownshadowing) | A local variable has the same name as a parameter, an outer local or a file-level object. | on |
| [`sca-own:missing-volatile`](#sca-ownmissing-volatile) | A file-level object is used by an interrupt handler and by other code, but is not declared volatile. | on |
| [`sca-own:internal-linkage`](#sca-owninternal-linkage) | A file-level function or object is visible to other files, but no included header declares it. | on |
| [`sca-own:dynamic-memory`](#sca-owndynamic-memory) | malloc, calloc, realloc or free (or new / delete) is used. | on |
| [`sca-own:magic-number`](#sca-ownmagic-number) | A numeric constant other than 0 or 1 appears in code without a name. | off |
| [`sca-own:empty-parameter-list`](#sca-ownempty-parameter-list) | A C function is declared with () instead of (void). | on |
| [`sca-own:unchecked-return`](#sca-ownunchecked-return) | The value a function returns (a status, a count, a flag) is thrown away. | on |

### sca-own:unused-variable

**Unused local variable.** A local variable is declared but never used.

*Why:* Unused variables are noise, and often a sign that the code does not do what was planned.

*Fix:* Remove the variable, or use it as intended.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
int len(const char *s)
{
    int checksum = 0;
    int n = 0;
    while (s[n] != 0) {
        n++;
    }
    return n;
}

/* follows the rule */
int len(const char *s)
{
    int n = 0;
    while (s[n] != 0) {
        n++;
    }
    return n;
}
```

### sca-own:unused-parameter

**Unused parameter.** A function parameter is never used.

*Why:* Either the function ignores input it should use, or the parameter is not needed.

*Fix:* Use the parameter, remove it, or write (void)name; when an interface requires it.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
void reset(int reason)
{
}

/* follows the rule */
void reset(int reason)
{
    (void)reason;
}
```

### sca-own:shadowing

**Name hides an outer name.** A local variable has the same name as a parameter, an outer local or a file-level object.

*Why:* Readers (and later edits) easily mix up the two variables.

*Fix:* Rename the inner variable.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
int sum(int len)
{
    int s = 0;
    {
        int len = 3;
        s = len;
    }
    return s + len;
}

/* follows the rule */
int sum(int len)
{
    int s = 0;
    {
        int part = 3;
        s = part;
    }
    return s + len;
}
```

### sca-own:missing-volatile

**Data shared with an interrupt is not volatile.** A file-level object is used by an interrupt handler and by other code, but is not declared volatile.

*Why:* Without volatile the compiler may keep the value in a register and never see the interrupt's change.

*Fix:* Declare the object volatile, and protect read-modify-write sequences against the interrupt.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
static unsigned int ticks;

void timer_isr(void)
{
    ticks++;
}

unsigned int ticks_now(void)
{
    return ticks;
}

/* follows the rule */
static volatile unsigned int ticks;

void timer_isr(void)
{
    ticks++;
}

unsigned int ticks_now(void)
{
    return ticks;
}
```

### sca-own:internal-linkage

**External name without a header declaration.** A file-level function or object is visible to other files, but no included header declares it.

*Why:* Either it is only used in this file (then it should be static) or other files declare it themselves, which lets declarations drift apart.

*Fix:* Make it static, or declare it in the module's header and include that header.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
int helper(int x)
{
    return x + 1;
}

/* follows the rule */
static int helper(int x)
{
    return x + 1;
}
```

### sca-own:dynamic-memory

**Dynamic memory.** malloc, calloc, realloc or free (or new / delete) is used.

*Why:* Heap use can fail or fragment at run time, so memory use is not known when the code is built.

*Fix:* Allocate statically (fixed-size arrays or pools).

```c
/* breaks the rule */
#include <stdlib.h>

int *make(void)
{
    return (int *)malloc(sizeof(int));
}

/* follows the rule */
static int storage;

int *make(void)
{
    return &storage;
}
```

### sca-own:magic-number

**Magic number.** A numeric constant other than 0 or 1 appears in code without a name.

*Why:* A name says what the number means and keeps every use in step when it changes.

*Fix:* Give the number a name with #define, an enum or a const object.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
int long_line(unsigned int len)
{
    return len > 24U;
}

/* follows the rule */
#define LINE_MAX 24U

int long_line(unsigned int len)
{
    return len > LINE_MAX;
}
```

### sca-own:empty-parameter-list

**Empty parameter list in C.** A C function is declared with () instead of (void).

*Why:* In C, () means "unknown arguments", so calls with wrong arguments are not checked.

*Fix:* Write (void).

```c
/* breaks the rule */
int answer()
{
    return 42;
}

/* follows the rule */
int answer(void)
{
    return 42;
}
```

### sca-own:unchecked-return

**Return value ignored.** The value a function returns (a status, a count, a flag) is thrown away.

*Why:* Errors reported through the return value then go unnoticed.

*Fix:* Check the value, or write (void)f(...); when ignoring it is intended.

```c
/* breaks the rule */
int nvm_read(int addr);

void load(void)
{
    nvm_read(4);
}

/* follows the rule */
int nvm_read(int addr);

int load(void)
{
    return nvm_read(4);
}
```

## Metrics

| Rule | What it finds | Default |
|---|---|---|
| [`his-metrics:cyclomatic`](#his-metricscyclomatic) | The number of decisions in a function plus one (if, loops, case, &&, ||, ?:) is above the limit. | on, limit 10 |
| [`his-metrics:nesting`](#his-metricsnesting) | Control statements are nested deeper than the limit. | on, limit 4 |
| [`his-metrics:statements`](#his-metricsstatements) | A function has more statements than the limit. | on, limit 50 |
| [`his-metrics:parameters`](#his-metricsparameters) | A function has more parameters than the limit. | on, limit 5 |
| [`his-metrics:returns`](#his-metricsreturns) | A function has more return points than the limit. | on, limit 1 |
| [`his-metrics:calls`](#his-metricscalls) | A function calls more different functions than the limit. | on, limit 7 |
| [`his-metrics:comment-density`](#his-metricscomment-density) | A file has fewer comment lines per code line than the limit. | on, limit 0.2 |

### his-metrics:cyclomatic

**Cyclomatic complexity.** The number of decisions in a function plus one (if, loops, case, &&, ||, ?:) is above the limit.

*Why:* Each decision adds a path to understand and to test; complex functions hide bugs.

*Fix:* Split the function into smaller ones, or simplify the logic (tables, early returns).

### his-metrics:nesting

**Nesting depth.** Control statements are nested deeper than the limit.

*Why:* Deep nesting is hard to read and usually means the function does too much.

*Fix:* Return early, or move inner blocks into functions.

### his-metrics:statements

**Function length.** A function has more statements than the limit.

*Why:* Long functions are hard to review and to test completely.

*Fix:* Split the function by task.

### his-metrics:parameters

**Number of parameters.** A function has more parameters than the limit.

*Why:* Many parameters are easy to mix up and suggest the function has too many jobs.

*Fix:* Group related parameters in a struct, or split the function.

### his-metrics:returns

**Number of return points.** A function has more return points than the limit.

*Why:* Several exits make it harder to see that every path cleans up and sets its results.

*Fix:* Use one exit at the end, or raise the limit if early returns are your style.

### his-metrics:calls

**Number of called functions.** A function calls more different functions than the limit.

*Why:* Many dependencies make a function hard to understand and to test in isolation.

*Fix:* Move groups of calls into helper functions.

### his-metrics:comment-density

**Comment density.** A file has fewer comment lines per code line than the limit.

*Why:* Code without comments says what it does, but not why.

*Fix:* Add comments that explain intent, units and limits.
